text:
George Epps and the Birmingham Affidavit Episode

How Leo Max Frank's defense investigators used a false name, a prize-fighter cover story, and a prearranged telephone call to get a sworn recantation from a teenage State witness

The Boy on the Streetcar

George W. Epps Jr. was fourteen years old when Mary Phagan was murdered on Saturday, April 26, 1913. He lived around the corner from the Phagan home and had known Mary for about a year.

He entered the case almost at once as the criminal investigation began to unfold. On Thursday, May 1, 1913, the Atlanta Constitution put his account on its front page under the headline "Frank Tried to Flirt With Murdered Girl Says Her Boy Chum." The paper reported Epps as saying Mary had told him about Leo Max Frank's conduct toward her and that she was afraid of him.1

That newspaper account should be kept apart from what Epps later swore at trial. In late July, on Monday the 28th day, 1913, he was called as the State's second witness, right after Mary's mother, Mrs. J. W. Coleman.2 According to the official Leo Frank Trial Brief of Evidence, he testified that he met Mary on the English Avenue streetcar at about ten minutes to twelve on Saturday, Confederate Memorial Day, sat with her, and left her at Forsyth and Marietta Streets at about seven minutes after twelve, whilst she went on to the National Pencil Company to get her pay. On cross-examination he said he judged the first time by the Bryant and Keheley clock and the second by the sun, a habit he picked up living in the country.3 

The defense fought that account in open court. On Friday, August 8, 1913, the Atlanta Journal reported the testimony of conductor W. T. Hollis and motorman W. M. Matthews. Both said Mary boarded alone. Neither remembered Epps riding with her.4

That was a real conflict in the evidence, and the jury heard both sides of it.

What happened to George Epps after the verdict was something else. The defense apparatus went after him with a vengeance.

"Terry"

Some time in the fall of 1913, a short, thin man began stopping Epps on the street in downtown Atlanta. Epps later described him as a man who "always wore a sour grin on his face." He said his name was Terry.5

His name was not Terry. It was J. W. Wrenn, and he was working for C. W. Burke, an investigator on the Frank defense side.

We know this from Burke himself. In an affidavit read at Frank's extraordinary-motion hearing in May 1914, Burke swore that "some time in September" 1913, Wrenn reported meeting Epps, and that the boy had supposedly "admitted part of his trial testimony was false and was afraid of Detective John Black." 

The Atlanta Journal then reported: "Burke swore he then instructed Wrenn to tell Epps he was Terry, a prize fighter, and was getting ready to go to New Orleans for a bout."6

The false name given Epps is admitted outright by the defense agent who was running the charade. 

Burke gave the instruction, and Wrenn's own affidavit corroborated Burke "in detail."6

The prize-fighter part needs some nuance. Burke admitted telling Wrenn to present himself to Epps as a prize fighter. He did not explain why, and no source located so far shows whether Wrenn had ever boxed. What the record proves is a false identity, "Terry," built around a prize-fighter and a New Orleans cover story that Burke himself authorized.

The New Orleans story is admitted too. Burke swore he told Wrenn to say he was getting ready to go to New Orleans for a bout. What Burke did not admit was promising Epps a place on that trip. That part comes from Epps.

Epps said Terry built up his trust over several meetings in front of the Aragon Hotel, then asked "if I did not want to travel with him." Terry said "he had a show company" and offered "$10.00 a week and expenses." He also told the boy "to keep this secret; not to let my father and mother or anybody know that I was going off." Epps did as he was told.5

Before the trip, Epps also saw Terry on Forsyth Street with another man, the man he would later know as "Kelly."5

The Night Train

On a Wednesday night in November 1913, most likely November 19, 1913, Terry gave Epps some of his old clothes and a dollar and told him to get a bath. Wrenn later confirmed the handout in his own affidavit, saying the boy was "ragged and filthy" when they met and that he gave him "some castoff clothing of his own to wear and also a dollar to get some food."5 6

At about 10:30 that night Epps met Terry at Forsyth and Hunter Streets. "He already had my ticket," Epps swore, and "said we were not going to New Orleans but were going to Birmingham."5 The Journal's summary of his affidavit puts it the same way: when he got ready to go, the man gave him a ticket "to Birmingham instead of New Orleans."7

At the Terminal Station, a man in glasses who "pretended he could not see good" asked Epps to help him down the steps. Wrenn later swore there was indeed "a blind man" on the train but that "the man was not Burke, but was some one Wrenn had never seen before."6 Who that man was is still unsettled. In his affidavit, Epps said the man in glasses looked like the one who "passed off as Kelly." The Journal's summary also reports Epps's opinion that the blind man was B. Bernard of Atlanta, the man he later named as the "chief."5 7

Burke and Austin G. Dennison, a New York detective working on the case, were on the same train. Burke swore that they "did not talk to them en route as they were in the day coach and he and Dennison were in the Pullman."6

So four people were going to Birmingham that night. Only one of them, a teenage boy, did not know who the other three were.

The Birmingham Hotel

The train reached Birmingham at about three in the morning.5

Two blocks from the station, a man grabbed Epps. According to Epps, the man said he had stolen "$10.00 from the Miller Minute Messenger Service" and "was going to take me to jail." The Journal's summary of Epps's affidavit says the man claimed to be a detective "of the Birmingham police department" and "placed him under arrest."5 7 The man called himself Kelly.

Burke admitted this contact in part only. He swore that after the train arrived, he "approached the other two and did talk with Epps about the money he had stolen from the messenger service." He also swore he was "very careful not to say or intimate at any time that he was an officer."6 His basis for the theft claim, he said, was Wrenn's report that the boy had confessed it to Terry. So we can see the manipulative shenanegans were already taking shape if the Epps account is to be believed. 

According to Epps, Terry told Kelly not to take him to jail but to the hotel. At the Birmingham Hotel, Terry offered to pay the boy's fine. Kelly said he would call the chief of detectives to see if he could take the money.5

This is where Burke's account and Epps's account meet.

Epps swore that Kelly "called him up, or pretended to call up," and then said the chief had another case against him: "perjury in the [Mary] Phagan case."5

Burke swore that he "told Epps he would phone to Atlanta about the money, but instead phoned Dennison by previous arrangement, and then told Epps that his (Burke's) chief was coming up to talk to him."6

That is not Epps's version. That is Burke's.

The call was fake. It was planned ahead of time. And the word "chief" came from Burke, not from a frightened boy's memory.

In the same affidavit, Burke said Dennison approached Epps "as one simply interested in the Frank case."6 

Those two statements do not fit well together. A boy who has just been accused of stealing, and who has just been told a call is being made about it, is then told the accuser's chief is on the way. Whatever Dennison said when he walked in, the boy had already been told who he was supposed to be.

The Statement

From here the two accounts split.

Epps swore that all three men "told me I had sworn a lie and had to come up and tell the truth or go to jail." He said they "got me over in the corner right at the window and pulled down the shades," that they "cursed John Black," and that "they kept talking to me and did not let me go to sleep all night." That's actually similar to an oldfashioned third-degree method where a prisoner is sleep deprived. The man they called the chief "commenced writing" and later came back "with him a stenographer."5

Burke's version is calmer. He said Dennison asked Epps to tell his story, and Epps repeated his trial testimony. When Dennison said he saw nothing wrong with it "if it is the truth," Epps answered, "Some of it was the truth, and some of it wasn't." Burke and Wrenn then left Dennison alone with the boy. When they came back, "Dennison had written out a three-page statement." Dennison read it to Epps, who Burke said made several corrections. "A stenographer was called in and the statement was dictated to him." Then "they took the boy before a notary and he swore to the affidavit."6

On one point, both men agree. George Epps did not write the Birmingham statement. Dennison did.

Epps added one more detail about the walk to the notary. "They took me by the jail," he said. In an office, "they made me hold up my right hand and swear to it." 

Epps said he signed because "they threatened me and I was scared and wanted to get back home." He also said he was told that if he refused he "would have to go to the Birmingham Reformatory," and that if he went back to Atlanta and changed his story, "Birmingham would fix me."5 

It was a signature under threat, after sleep deprivation and promise that if he repudiated the statement he would be sent to the Birmingham Reformatory.

Burke denied coercion. The Journal reported that the boy "was made absolutely no promise of reward, nor was he coerced in any way, Burke swears."6

This would be a reported pattern by witnesses of the defense tactics, followed the defense denying it. 

Coming Home

The next day Terry moved Epps to the Empire Hotel. There, Epps said, Terry "got two telegrams and he claimed they were from Atlanta and that the show had to come back to Atlanta before we could go to New Orleans."5 Even on the way out of Alabama, the New Orleans story was kept alive.

They left Birmingham at about three in the morning and reached Atlanta at about seven a.m. Before they arrived, Terry gave the boy a dollar and a half and told him to go to the Gate City Hotel "and stay there and don't let anybody see me." They likely didn't want the authorities questioning him about the authenticity of the false affidavit he had deposed. Later he gave him another dollar and a half "in nickles and dimes and told me to go out to the football game."5

Epps's father later swore that his son came home on Saturday, November 22, 1913, saying a boxer named Terry had taken him to Birmingham on Wednesday night "to make a boxer" of him. He said he knew nothing about the trip until he heard from Birmingham.8 The boy's own timeline fits that date: a Wednesday-night departure, the statement sworn on Thursday producing a defense favorable affidavit, the move to the Empire Hotel on Friday, and a Saturday-morning return with a football game that afternoon.

The ten dollars a week was never paid in whole or part.

Milledgeville

About three weeks after he got back, Epps was brought before Judge Tindall in the juvenile court. The judge was willing to put him on probation. Epps asked to be sent to the State Reformatory at Milledgeville instead.

His reason: he was afraid that if he stayed in Atlanta, and took back the Birmingham statement, "they would take me to Birmingham and put me in jail for signing the statement over there."5

A boy who asks to be locked up rather than stay where those men could find him is telling us how scared he was at the time. The wild goose chase to Alabama by train after being told originally they were going to New Orleans, then with hotel hopping, the sleep deprivation, the psychological games, and the threats, all took a toll on the young boy.

At Milledgeville, defense attorney, Stiles Hopkins, came to see Epps.

According to Epps, Hopkins "told Capt. Lovvorn he wanted to see me; that they had an affidavit which I had made in Birmingham and they wanted me to sign it." 

Epps compared the copies, agreed "that was the same one," and signed.5 

Hopkins's own affidavit, read by the defense in May, 1914, says he went to Milledgeville "in February or March" with an affidavit "to read to George Epps."7

The re-signed statement is dated Friday, February 27, 1914, pinpointing the date. It was attested by J. Cleveland Cooper, clerk of the superior court.7

Dennison's Birmingham text now had a Georgia oath on it, with a new date and most importantly eye witnesses to it that were reputable.

The Recantation Goes Public Less Than a Week Later

On Wednesday, March 4, 1914, the Atlanta Georgian printed the affidavit at length. In it, Epps said he had sworn falsely at the inquest and at trial, blamed Detective John Black for persuading him, and accused Solicitor Hugh Dorsey of encouraging it.11

The next day Adolph Ochs' The New York Times carried the story to the whole country under the headline:

 "Lied Against Frank, a Newsboy Swears."12

Epps was a former Newsie who shouted headlines from the street corners of Atlanta and collected Indian head and new Lincoln pennies from prospective buyers.

Neither paper told its readers the statement began as three pages drafted by a defense investigator in an Alabama hotel room, after the boy had been brought there by a man operating under a false name and dangling a bogus job offer. This was no ordinary witness interview. The false identity, invented employment opportunity, secret trip, hotel-room setting, and investigator-written statement gave the entire episode the appearance of a carefully staged psychological operation, a psyop built around deception from the start.

The Epps Family Answers in the Atlanta Press

Epps's father answered right away. On Thursday, March 5, 1914, the Atlanta Constitution reported his statement calling his son's affidavit a falsehood and saying the boy had told him about riding with Mary Phagan before any detective was involved. 

The same article carried Detective Black's denial and a rebuttal from Chief of Detectives Newport Lanford.9 

The Atlanta Journal ran the father's statement the same day, along with defense attorney Stiles Hopkins's explanation of how the affidavit was obtained.10

On Sunday, March 8, the Constitution published sworn statements from the father and from an uncle, named in the press as both Henry Epps and W. H. Epps, respectively. The uncle had gone to Milledgeville and reported that George said he had been trapped and that his July 28, 1913, trial testimony was the truth.8

The father's affidavit does two things. It shows the Terry story was known in the family months before the May hearing, so nobody made it up newfangled for that hearing. And it goes straight at the published affidavit's main claim, that Detective Black created the boy's story, because the father said George told the trolley ride to downtown Atlanta at home first.

Epps Takes It Back

On Friday morning, May 1, 1914, Epps was brought to Atlanta from Milledgeville. That day, with N. A. Garner beside him, he watched a man come out of the National Pencil Company factory and pointed him out as Kelly. Garner told him the man was known in Atlanta as C. W. Burke.5 

It was at that moment in time clarified for Garner that Kelly was the alias of Burke.

"I am now prepared to say, and do say under oath," Epps swore, "that he is the man who was with me in Birmingham, passing under the name of Kelly."5

On Monday, May 4, 1914, he gave Solicitor Dorsey his full account. He said his trial testimony was true and described Terry, the trip, Kelly, the hotel, the chief, the statement, and his fear of being taken back. He signed every page and closed with the words "I am now just 15 years old."5

The Atlanta Journal reported it on Tuesday, May 5, 1914, under the headline "Many Sensations Sprung by Dorsey at Frank Hearing." The Journal's summary said Epps now believed Terry was Jimmie Wrenn, Kelly was C. W. Burke, and the chief was B. Bernard of Atlanta.7 Its summary also gave the claimed theft as $12, where Epps's affidavit says $10.00. 5, 7,

Burke’s Answer

Burke’s affidavit concerning George Epps was dated Tuesday, May 5, 1914. On Wednesday, May 6, The Atlanta Journal reported it alongside J. W. Wrenn’s affidavit under the headline “Frank Loses Fight for New Trial,” with the subhead “Judge Hill Denies Motion as Defense Closes Arguments.” Later the same afternoon, Judge Benjamin H. Hill denied Frank’s extraordinary motion for a new trial.6

Epps then answered Burke point by point in another sworn statement preserved in the Georgia Supreme Court record. He flatly denied telling Wrenn his testimony was false. He denied saying he intended to take “a hobo trip.” He denied claiming fear kept him from giving an affidavit in Atlanta. Of Burke’s account, Epps said every statement attributed to him was “absolutely and unqualifiedly false.” If Wrenn had supplied Burke with those claims, Epps said, Wrenn had invented them.

Epps also rejected any suggestion of an innocent or casual conversation with Wrenn in Atlanta. Wrenn, he swore, “did not discuss the Frank case with witness casually or otherwise in Atlanta but decoyed witness out of the city and out of the state to discuss it with him.”5

The Admitted Deception

The strongest part of the Epps episode does not depend on believing everything Epps said.

The whole deception depends in part on what Burke swore.

Burke admitted telling Wrenn to call himself Terry. Wrenn's name was not Terry.

Burke admitted telling Wrenn to present himself as a prize fighter getting ready to go to New Orleans for a bout.

Burke admitted that he and defense operative, Dennison, rode the same train to Birmingham, in the Pullman, and did not talk to Epps and Wrenn on the way.

Burke admitted raising the messenger-service money with Epps after they arrived.

Burke admitted telling Epps he would telephone Atlanta about that money, calling Dennison instead by previous arrangement, and then telling Epps that his chief was coming.

Burke admitted that Dennison wrote a three-page statement, that it was dictated to a stenographer, and that Epps was taken before a notary and sworn to it.

Wrenn corroborated all of it "in detail."6

So did the defense admit wrongdoing? It admitted deliberate deception. It did not admit coercion or anything illegal such as subornation of perjury. 

Burke acknowledged authorizing the false Terry identity, the prize-fighter pretext, and New Orleans cover story, the separate travel to Birmingham, and the prearranged telephone call, and he offered no explanation or apology for any of it. He did not call these steps wrong. He did not call them proper either. He simply described them and swore the boy was neither coerced nor promised a reward.6

What Burke did not admit: a false arrest, threats, sleep deprivation, a perjury accusation, or posing as a police officer. He expressly denied three things: coercion, any promise of reward, and presenting himself as an officer. The Journal's report shows no specific answer to Epps's claims that he was arrested and kept awake all night.6

The deception is documented by the man who ran it. The coercion is disputed.

Where the Evidence Stops

The Epps record does not settle whether his streetcar times were right. The conductor and motorman contested them at trial, and the jury weighed that.4 And the evidence suggested that Mary arrived closer to noon. But in 1913, clocks could be off a number of minutes in any direction.

It does not prove the threats, the mock arrest, the sleepless night, the pulled shades, or the warnings about the Birmingham Reformatory. Those rest on Epps's sworn word, backed by his father's and uncle's statements, his identification of Burke, and the circumstances.

It does not prove who the blind man was, or who the "chief" was. Burke said Dennison. Epps named Bernard.

And it does not prove Wrenn never boxed. It proves he was told to say he did, under a name that was not his.

If Burke's own starting point is accepted in full, and the boy really had told Terry that part of his testimony was false, one question is still left open. Why did it take a false name, a prize-fighter story, a trip out of state, investigators riding in another car, a bogus theft accusation, a fake phone call, a guy pretending to be blind, and a statement written by someone else to get that boy to swear it under oath? A witness who wants to take back his testimony can be walked into a lawyer's office in Atlanta.

The Record Since

In March 1914, readers across the country were told a State witness had confessed to lying. By May, the national press was reporting the other side. On May 5, The New York Times ran "Frank Affidavits False, Says Dorsey."13 On May 6, it reported that the defense's methods for getting affidavits might go before a grand jury.14 The Georgia papers printed far more of the Birmingham detail than those short national stories did.

The March version has held on. A 2025 overview of the case in The Saturday Evening Post says Epps "recanted, stating both his testimony at the inquest and during the trial had been coerced by the police's lead investigator." It says nothing about Birmingham, Terry, Burke, Dennison, or Epps's sworn reaffirmation in May 1914.15

More than a hundred years later, the recantation is still being repeated without the story of how it was obtained.

What the Epps Record Proves

C. W. Burke's name comes up again and again in the disputed affidavits of Frank's post-conviction campaign. Albert McKnight, Ivey Jones, Mary Rich, Aaron Allen, Frank Reese, Fred Perkerson, and others later complained of false pretenses, prepared statements, inducements, or pressure to change their evidence. The Epps episode does not prove any of those complaints. Each one has to be tested on its own documents.

There is already one link in the defense's own filings. In an affidavit read at the same May 1914 hearing, Wrenn described taking R. P. Barrett to the Kimball House, where he "introduced Burke to him as Kelly."7 The alias Epps said Burke used in Birmingham was, by Wrenn's own sworn account, used again with another man in the case.

That is what George Epps gives us: one episode where the investigator himself swore to the method. A false name. A cover story. Investigators out of sight on the same train. A fake phone call. A "chief." A statement written by someone else and sworn before a notary.

When another witness describes something like that, we can hold it up against what Burke swore he did to a teenage boy in Birmingham in November 1913, and test it document by document.

Sidney Starr Files New Motion for Bond, Says Inmates Are Pressuring Her for Money and Her TV Fame Makes Her Recognizable Behind Bars

The reality TV personality has filed a new Motion for Bond in Fulton County Superior Court, asking a judge to set bond and schedule a hearing at the earliest available date.

Starr, 38, has been in custody at the Fulton County Jail since her Aug. 2 arrest. In the new filing, her attorneys argue that she does not pose a significant risk of fleeing, failing to appear in court or posing a danger to the community.

Her legal team also points to Starr’s lack of a criminal history and her ties to Georgia. According to the motion, Starr has lived in the Chicago area her entire life, but has a cousin in Hampton, Georgia, and a friend with a home in Decatur who has offered to let Starr stay there if she is released.

But the filing also details what her attorneys say has been happening to Starr behind bars.

According to the motion, Starr is an actress who works in television and is “recognizable to a sizeable portion of the Jail population.” Her attorneys claim she has been continually pressured by other inmates for money.

The filing also alleges that Starr’s personal identification number for the jail’s video communication system was stolen and used by other inmates.

Her attorneys say the situation has taken a toll on Starr while she remains in custody, citing alleged adverse effects on her physical and mental health.

The motion says Starr is willing to accept strict conditions if the court grants her bond. Her attorneys state that she would agree to home confinement, electronic monitoring and restrictions involving social media.

The filing also includes letters from Starr’s father, Herbert Favors, and longtime friend Everett Foney. According to the motion, both letters speak to Starr’s character, family responsibilities and willingness to comply with court requirements if released.

Starr’s attorneys also argue that continued incarceration is affecting her ability to work. Before her arrest, the motion says, she earned income through television and social media and helped care for her mother, with whom she had been living in Chicago.

A judge has not yet ruled on the new request.

text:
The Tight End Tackled by Trust: Travis Kelce Named in a $35 Million Ponzi Scheme

Kansas City Chiefs star Travis Kelce learned this month that even Super Bowl rings and a high-profile marriage offer no shield against a polished liar. Prosecutors named him among 64 victims when Siddharth Jawahar received an 11-year prison sentence and a $31.35 million restitution order. The exact sum Kelce lost remains sealed. What is public is the scale of the operation: Jawahar’s Swiftarc Capital collected more than $35 million from 2016 to 2023 yet placed only about $10 million into actual investments.
Jawahar sold the image of a sophisticated fund. Instead he parked nearly 99 percent of client money in a single holding, Philip Morris Pakistan, a concentration that violated his own stated limits. When that stock cratered, he did not disclose the damage. He reported phantom gains and used cash from later investors to keep earlier ones quiet, the classic Ponzi loop. The leftover millions financed private jets, Gucci and Prada shopping, luxury apartments, and expensive dinners. A 2021 Forbes piece had already listed Kelce alongside NBA players Gary Harris, Tim Hardaway Jr., and Mason Plumlee as investors in a related Swiftarc fund, suggesting the introduction traveled through athlete networks rather than cold calls. Texas regulators canceled Swiftarc’s registration in June 2022 and posted a public cease-and-desist order. The warning sat in plain sight, yet the scheme continued because trust in familiar names replaced ordinary due diligence.
Kelce has not spoken publicly. No one has accused him of wrongdoing. His reported net worth and Taylor Swift’s fortune make a single undisclosed loss unlikely to change his lifestyle or his remaining seasons on the field. The episode still carries weight. It shows how affinity fraud works: a teammate or acquaintance vouches, the paperwork looks official, and the red flags stay unread. Future deals will almost certainly face harder questions from his team. Restitution may eventually return some money, but the larger cost is the reminder that fame attracts both genuine opportunity and people who treat that fame as inventory.

Trump’s Top 25 Achievements: The List Every Conservative Should Know and Use Donald Trump doesn’t have an accomplishment problem. Republicans have an information problem. It’s on each of us to change that. With the midterms coming, an astonishing number of Republican voters cannot name three things President Trump has accomplished. Which is remarkable when you consider that Donald Trump has accomplished more in a year and a half than any other president ever did in four.  Indeed, he has accomplished so much, so fast, across so many fronts that most people cannot keep up. The Enemedia buries the victories, while Republicans do an abysmal job of explaining them.  So here is the cheat sheet. It barely scratches the surface. And yet each and every item here is a game-changer, and your befuddled black-pilling friends need to know it.  This is not a list of promises. It’s a list of laws enacted, cases won, policies implemented, agreements secured, and measurable results.  You don’t have to memorize all 25. Learn five. And when somebody says Trump “hasn’t done much,” show them the receipts.  Trump Restored American Safety and Sovereignty 1. He made the border a real border again. In a matter of months, Trump reduced illegal border crossings to their lowest level in half a century. Catch-and-release is finished. The wall is going up and even being expanded, “Remain in Mexico” is back, and the Administration reduced releases into the country by an incredible 99.9 percent.  2. He reversed mass migration.America recorded negative net migration in 2025 for the first time in at least half a century. So far, nearly 3 million illegal aliens have left the country, whether voluntarily or involuntarily: more than 675,000 forcibly deported and the rest “self-deported.”   Many of those self-deportations were facilitated by the President’s innovative program to offer plane tickets and cash bonuses for illegals to leave, not only incentivizing good behavior but significantly reducing the cost of deportations. Citizenship and the law actually mean something again.  3. He signed the Laken Riley Act — and required detention of criminal illegal aliens.Named for an innocent girl murdered by an illegal alien, the Laken Riley Act requires federal authorities to detain illegals arrested for theft, burglary, shoplifting, assaulting police, or any crime causing death or serious injury. It also lets states sue officials who refuse to enforce it.  Laken Riley should still be alive. This law will prevent tragedies like hers.  4. History’s biggest drop in violent crime, and the lowest violent crime rate in 126 years.According to FBI data, violent crime in America dropped an incredible 9.7 percent in 2025 — the largest one-year decline in history. Murder fell 18.1 percent, robbery fell 18.5 percent. And America’s violent crime rate is its lowest since 1900.  This is what happens when you put the National Guard on the streets in crime-ridden blue cities: fewer victims, safer streets, and better futures for America’s poorest.  Trump Launched an American Industrial Supercycle 5. He made the 2017 tax cuts permanent…and better.The One Big Beautiful Bill locked in the largest tax cut in modern history, including the doubled standard deduction, the expanded Child Tax Credit, and 100 percent expensing for factories and equipment. It also delivered No Tax on Tips, No Tax on Overtime, an abolition of most taxes on Social Security benefits, and major relief for seniors.  Every Democrat voted no. With the 2017 act set to expire in December 2025, that would have resulted in the largest tax hike in American history.  6. He repealed 129 regulations for every new one. In fiscal 2025, federal agencies finalized 646 deregulatory actions and just five regulatory actions: 129-to-1, and in nearly every case, the “one” was to repeal the others! OIRA says the savings exceeded those of Trump’s entire first term. That is more freedom, lower costs, and less bureaucratic sabotage.  Of these, the crown jewel was the repeal of Obama’s 2009 “Endangerment Finding”, the legal foundation for the Green New Scam’s vehicle mandates. EPA calls it the largest deregulatory action in American history and estimates that by itself, it will save Americans more than $1.3 trillion. Trump also killed the federal EV mandate, restored Americans’ freedom to buy the cars and trucks they actually want, and even eliminated the incentives behind the almost universally hated start-stop button.  7. He secured $18 trillion in announced investment commitments.That’s nearly two-thirds the size of the entire American economy, building American factories, chip plants, data centers, energy projects, steel mills, shipyards, and supply chains employing American workers. Apple, Meta, NVIDIA, Micron, Hyundai, U.S. Steel, Ford, Taiwan Semiconductor, and many corporations and sovereign wealth funds are betting big on Trump’s America.   No President has ever done anything remotely like it. And it’s just getting started.  8. He made “reshoring” and “reindustrialization” real, not a slogan. Ford is moving Lincoln production out of China. Toyota is shifting Tacoma production from Mexico to Texas. GM, Honda, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and others are expanding U.S. production. The capital equipment pouring into the country is the machinery that’s building the growing boom.  9. He replaced lopsided trade deals with balanced, reciprocal trade.Trump used tariffs as leverage to reverse 80 years of lopsided trade deals that favored everyone but America, and to win new or improved agreements with trading partners accounting for more than half of global GDP. Those agreements open foreign markets, attack non-tariff barriers, defend strategic industries, and make it more profitable to build in America than to export American jobs.  10. He shifted global energy dominance from the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of America.Once the world’s largest energy importer — “exporting” $700 billion a year to our enemies — America now outproduces Saudi Arabia and Russia combined. The U.S. is also setting new records in oil, natural gas, and LNG exports, becoming the first country ever to export more than 100 million metric tons of LNG in a year.  Trump also opened land, accelerated permits, expanded pipelines and export terminals, and made American energy a tool for prosperity and peace.  11. After four decades of nuclear paralysis, Trump brought five new reactors online in a single year.For more than 40 years, not one new privately developed non-light-water reactor reached criticality in America. Trump ordered at least three by July 4, 2026. DOE delivered four by the deadline, then a fifth just one month later.  Decades of zero. One Trump summer: five. That is a genuine nuclear renaissance.  Trump Made Elections Matter Again 12. He broke the Deep State’s power to defy the elected branches. In Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court ruled for the first time in 90 years that Article 2, Section 1 is still part of the Constitution: the President may fire subordinate officials in the executive branch, overturning the 1935 precedent that insulated “independent” agencies from voters’ control.  Ever wonder why elections often seem to change nothing? How about one President and 5,000 political appointees vs. 2.8 million unfireable, unaccountable bureaucrats? THAT is the “Deep State”.  Trump then made that victory real. For the first time in a century, all policy-making bureaucrats can now be fired for misconduct, incompetence, or defying lawful directives. The permanent bureaucracy no longer gets to veto the voters.  13. He ended nationwide injunction abuse. In Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court sharply limited nationwide injunctions. A single, local, district judge should not be able to block a national policy for everyone, everywhere; and yet that’s exactly what they’ve done, nonstop, ever since Trump (and only Trump) took office in 2017.   In restricting that unconstitutional power, the Court kneecapped the Black Robe Bureaucracy’s favorite tool of unlawful judicial supremacy.  14. He shut down USAID as a left-wing slush fund and shadow government.USAID had become a taxpayer-funded machine for exporting abortion, gender ideology, censorship, and left-wing politics. It had a bigger budget than the CIA and the State Department combined, absolutely no accountability whatsoever, and a penchant for overthrowing governments.  Trump terminated it — completely — and moved real humanitarian aid under the State Department. Immediately, seven socialist Latin American governments lost re-election. Coincidence?  15. He shrank Federal employment to its lowest level in 60 years.From a high under Biden, the federal workforce is now its smallest since 1966. Workforce reductions, agency closures, and spending cancellations mean fewer bureaucrats paid to resist the voters.  What’s more, when Biden left office, 94 percent of federal employees “worked” from home. The Trump administration cracked down: as Elon Musk put it, “you can work from the office or you can pretend to work somewhere else.”  16. He expelled DEI from the federal government.Trump eliminated federal DEI offices and barred race- and sex-based preferences across the executive branch. Government hiring and contracting are returning to merit and equality under the law, ending the grotesque Democrat idea that “fighting discrimination” requires the federal government to discriminate.  He Defended Faith and Family 17. He delivered sweeping pro-life reform. In his first term, Trump delivered the judges that overturned the abominable Roe v. Wade. Hardly anyone believed it could be done, or that Trump would do it. But he did, and a half-century nightmare finally ended.  Since returning to office, Trump has enforced the Hyde Amendment prohibiting the use of federal funds to pay for abortions, reinstated and expanded the Mexico City Policy prohibiting federal funding of foreign abortions, ended federal fetal-tissue research, strengthened conscience protections, protected Medicaid from funding large abortion providers, and pardoned 23 pro-life activists prosecuted by Biden’s weaponized Justice Department.  He’s also done everything within the Executive Branch’s power to defund Planned Parenthood. It would be nice if Congress did likewise.  No President has ever done more to protect life. No one.  18. He got men out of women’s sports, and restored biological reality to federal policy.The United States government once again officially recognizes two sexes: male and female. Trump ended federal support for the chemical and surgical gender mutilation of children, stopped taxpayer funding of such irreversible abominations, and forced more than three dozen health systems to end or suspend their programs as well.  Trump also enforced Title IX as written: women and girls deserve their own teams, trophies, scholarships, and locker rooms. The NCAA and other athletic organizations changed their rules in response. After years of Democrats doing everything they could to destroy women’s sports and ruin girls’ lives, Trump’s administration protects women and girls again.  19. He enacted America’s first nationwide school-choice program — and launched Trump Accounts. As part of the President’s One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump enacted America’s first-ever nationwide school choice program. The new Education Freedom Tax Credit helps fund scholarships for tuition, books, and other educational costs.  That’s on top of the new Trump Accounts, which give every child a tax-advantaged stake in America’s future, including a $1,000 federal seed for eligible newborns. Parents gain power. Bureaucracies lose it. And children learn first-hand about free markets and future orientation.  20. He targeted anti-Christian bias and discrimination.Trump created the White House Faith Office, Religious Liberty Commission, and Task Force to Eradicate Anti-Christian Bias. He restored conscience protections and made clear that Christians do not surrender their First Amendment rights merely by entering public life.  He Restored Peace Through Strength and Put America First 21. He forced NATO to stop freeloading and increase defense spending by 250 percent.For decades, wealthy European governments underfunded their militaries, effectively sending America the bill and using American taxpayers to subsidize their bloated welfare states. Trump forced NATO to replace its old two-percent-of-GDP spending target with an enormous five percent by 2035.  Allied spending is rising, American defense orders are soaring, and Europe is becoming a partner instead of a dependent.  22. He drove China out of the Caribbean.China spent years building strategic beachheads at both ends of the Panama Canal, in Cuba, and in Maduro’s Venezuela. Trump forced Panama out of Belt and Road, expanded American security access around the Canal, and captured Maduro, who now sits in a New York jail cell awaiting trial.  Beijing’s planned encirclement of the United States collapsed. The Monroe Doctrine is back. Call it the Donroe Doctrine.  23. He brokered eight peace deals in just eight months. In eight months, Trump brokered peace in eight conflicts spanning four continents, including wars that had gone on for as much as 40 years. It’s a record unmatched by any other President.  24. He launched and funded Golden Dome, the first-ever true missile defense for the U.S. population.Ronald Reagan dreamed of making nuclear missiles obsolete through his Strategic Defense Initiative. Today, Trump is actually building it: a layered homeland shield with space-based sensors and interceptors, conventional defenses, and new technologies including microwave systems to destroy drone swarms and directed-energy weapons (yes, lasers) that can replace an $11 million missile with $2 of electricity.  Congress has funded the initial $25 billion, with far more on the way once it passes the NDAA this fall. Better a shield than a sword.  25. He restored the warrior ethos — and reversed the recruiting crisis.After years of missed targets under Biden, every active military component met or exceeded its 2025 recruiting goal. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth refocused the newly renamed Department of War on actually winning wars, while pouring resources into shipbuilding, munitions, drones, missile defense, and America’s atrophied industrial base.  Young Americans once again believe their Commander-in-Chief is worth serving. And they’re showing up en masse.  Now Act Like It Matters Those are not tweets or campaign promises. They are changes in law, power, investment, sovereignty, culture, and the structure of the Republic itself. And they’re just the top 25: I could give you hundreds more.  Midterms are turnout elections. We do not need to convince Democrats to love Donald Trump. We need Republicans and friendly independents to understand what is at stake — and to show up.  And let’s be clear. When you say (as some of you will) “the Republicans need to do a good enough job telling this story”, you’re pointing at yourself. You are “the Republicans.” The Democrats don’t rely exclusively on their elected officials to tell their story: everyone from their media lackeys to their lowest-level supporters are constantly spreading their “news”, whatever that “news” happens to be.  Today’s conservatives have more ability to find whatever you want to know than any group of people in human history, yet half of them couldn’t name any of the accomplishments in this essay, and if they were to read it, they would just complain that something else they wanted hasn’t happened fast enough to suit them.  This is called “black-pilling.” It’s a loser mindset, and if you engage in it, you deserve to lose: horribly, painfully, personally. And guess what: you will, unless people who are serious step up to save you. Which is frankly pathetic, but for the rest of our sakes, necessary.  So tell people our story. Donald Trump is delivering great things, whether or not heaven on earth has broken out quite yet. Do the work, send the team he needs to Washington to finish the job, and get ready for 2028 afterward.

text:
Researchers Build Post-Quantum Defense for Lightning

Researchers at East Texas A&M University have developed PQLN, a research prototype designed to protect Bitcoin Lightning’s off-chain communications from future quantum attacks.

PQLN adds post-quantum cryptography to Lightning’s gossip, invoices, offers and payment routing while keeping existing nodes and Bitcoin consensus unchanged.

The system uses NIST’s ML-DSA and ML-KEM standards alongside existing Lightning cryptography. Researchers found the main trade-off was bandwidth, with gossip traffic increasing by around 10×.

The important part: PQLN protects Lightning’s off-chain messaging, not the BTC locked in payment channels. Making those funds quantum-safe would still require changes at the Bitcoin base layer.

PQLN is currently a research implementation, not a live network-wide upgrade.

What are people encountering when they report a winged figure with piercing eyes in the darkness? Join Rissa Miller and Lon Strickler on Saturday, September 26, 2026, at approximately noon at the Albatwitch Harvest Festival at the Columbia Crossing River Trails Center in Columbia, Pennsylvania, for “Eyes in the Dark: The Haunting Legacy of the Mothman.”

Our presentation explores the unsettling sightings that made Point Pleasant, West Virginia, synonymous with Mothman. We’ll examine witness accounts, the stories surrounding the creature, and how a local mystery grew into one of America’s most enduring paranormal legends.

The story also takes us deeper into Point Pleasant’s history, from the 1768 Treaty of Fort Stanwix and the 1774 Battle of Point Pleasant to the life and death of Shawnee leader Chief Cornstalk. We’ll discuss his efforts toward peace, his murder at Fort Randolph, and the alleged “dying curse” later woven into Mothman folklore, distinguishing documented history from legend.

From Point Pleasant, we’ll turn to the more recent Chicago Mothman sightings and encounters. These reports of winged humanoids raise intriguing questions about what witnesses are seeing and whether the similarities between accounts suggest a connection, or reflect the influence of a familiar legend.

We’ll also bring the discussion closer to home with sightings and encounters reported in south-central Pennsylvania. Exploring these regional accounts alongside the Point Pleasant and Chicago reports offers a broader look at the experiences people describe and the mysteries that remain.

Whether you’re fascinated by cryptids, drawn to local history, or curious about an unusual experience of your own, join us for a journey through eyewitness reports, historical events, and haunting folklore. We look forward to seeing you at approximately noon on September 26 for “Eyes in the Dark: The Haunting Legacy of the Mothman.”

THIS IS HOW POPULAR ANTI-WAR INFLUENCERS SUDDENLY BECAME ZELENSKY’S PUPPETS

United24 is a Ukrainian government initiative Volodymyr Zelenskyy created after the 2022 war with Russia. Its stated mission is to unite individuals, companies, and partners in support of Ukraine.

But the war did not only unfold on the battlefield. It also launched an information war, one where separating fact from fiction became increasingly difficult.

Remember the “Ghost of Kyiv”? Viral videos claimed a lone Ukrainian fighter pilot had shot down as many as six Russian aircraft. The story spread worldwide before it was revealed to be false.

Investigative journalist Elizabeth Lane reports that Ukraine’s messaging campaign may have gone beyond viral stories and social-media trolling.

As per her reporting, American veterans, including former special operations personnel with YouTube channels and other platforms, were offered money and access in exchange for producing pro-Ukraine content.
Some were reportedly offered up to $10,000.

Lane says United24, a state-backed Ukrainian fundraising and communications initiative, made the offers. One influencer appears to acknowledge the arrangement on camera.

If true, that raises serious questions. American donations, taxpayer dollars, and other support flow into United24, while the organization may also be funding messaging meant to shape American views of the war.

@imelizabethlane investigated the operation and the question at its center: are American taxpayer dollars being used to fund a covert influence campaign that advances pro-Ukraine narratives and sustains support for the war?

Again Wrong, not sure where you are getting for info from. but here are the facts. 

1947 UN Partition Plan
The UN proposed two states. Jewish leadership accepted it. Arab leadership rejected it and went to war. That was the first formal two-state offer.

Camp David 2000 and Clinton Parameters
Prime Minister Ehud Barak and President Clinton put a detailed package on the table, a Palestinian state on roughly 97% of the West Bank plus all of Gaza, land swaps for the rest, a Palestinian capital in Arab neighborhoods of East Jerusalem, and limited refugee return plus compensation. 
Arafat walked away without a counter-offer that closed the deal. The Second Intifada started weeks later.

Olmert 2008
Ehud Olmert showed Mahmoud Abbas a map, Israel would annex about 6.8% of the West Bank (mainly settlement blocs), swap roughly equivalent land from Israel proper, give all of Gaza, create a link between Gaza and the West Bank, and divide Jerusalem with an international committee over the Holy Basin. Olmert told Abbas to sign it. Abbas did not.

These were not “caveats instead of a state.” They were offers of a state with borders, a capital, and land swaps. Palestinians rejected them, just as they rejected 1947.

Look at the maps and numbers from Camp David/Clinton Parameters and Olmert 2008 instead of treating Netanyahu’s later statements as the entire history. Those documents exist. They offered a Palestinian state with defined territory. The record is that Palestinian leaders did not accept them

The 2005 withdrawal was real
Israel removed every settlement and every soldier from inside Gaza. More than 8,000 settlers were moved. The IDF left the Strip. 
That is not “moving the guards to the outer wall.” After Israel left, the Palestinian Authority ran Gaza until Hamas won the 2006 election and then violently seized the territory from Fatah in 2007.

Why the blockade started
The blockade (enforced by Israel and Egypt at Rafah) began after Hamas took power, not after the 2005 pullout. 
Hamas’s charter called for Israel’s destruction. 
It immediately used Gaza to fire rockets and smuggle weapons. Israel restricted goods, cement, steel pipes, fertilizers, certain machinery—because Hamas turns them into rockets and tunnels. That is a security policy against an armed group that took over after Israel left, not a decision to keep Gaza as a prison from day one

Some consumer goods were restricted in 2007–2010 and later eased. Chocolate, toys, notebooks, and spices appeared on tight lists for a period; they were not a permanent ban on food or medicine.

The Gaza airport was already damaged during the Second Intifada and was not rebuilt because Hamas would have used it for weapons.

Mowing the lawn

Those operations followed thousands of rockets fired at Israeli towns once Israel was no longer inside Gaza. They were not unprovoked lawn-mowing of a quiet enclave.

Great March of Return

Hamas later acknowledged that a large share of those killed were its own members. Some protesters were unarmed, others approached or tried to breach the fence, threw explosives, and launched incendiary kites. 
Israel used live fire and produced high casualties; that use of force was widely criticized. It was not a purely peaceful, unarmed demonstration met with random shooting.

text:
DoubleZero Edge x Hyperliquid

@doublezero has added Hyperliquid market data to its Edge data platform.

The announcement is really about the data layer underneath an active onchain market: how detailed order-book updates are distributed, reconstructed, and made available to systems monitoring market activity.

According to DoubleZero, Edge now distributes data across:

• Hyperliquid’s native perpetual markets
• trade[XYZ] HIP-3 markets

The launch covers four feeds across two data levels:

• Market by Order (MBO)
• Top of Book (TOB)

And across both market groups.

The distinction matters.

A top-of-book feed shows the best available bid and offer at a given point in time.

Market-by-order data goes much deeper, providing order-level events that allow software to reconstruct the state and evolution of the order book.

For systems analysing market activity, that additional depth can provide more context around how orders enter, change, and leave the book.

But detailed data is only useful if it can be delivered and reconstructed reliably.

That makes network architecture part of the data-quality conversation.

DoubleZero says Edge uses multicast distribution over dedicated fiber paths.

Multicast allows one data stream to be distributed efficiently to multiple recipients, while dedicated network paths are designed to reduce reliance on public internet routing.

DoubleZero contrasts this architecture with public WebSocket delivery and says Edge provides machine-readable data with no per-stream caps.

These are DoubleZero’s architectural and product claims. The announcement does not provide an independent benchmark demonstrating a universal latency advantage across every location, workload, or network environment.

The same applies to the “fastest commercially available feed” language: that should be treated as DoubleZero’s claim, not as an independently established fact.

There’s also an important distinction between coverage and completeness.

DoubleZero describes the announced Edge coverage as uncapped, covering every market and order with full L4 order-book detail.

That means the focus is not simply on seeing the best price. It is on receiving the underlying order-level events needed to maintain a much more complete representation of market state.

For an onchain venue with many instruments and frequent order updates, that becomes an infrastructure problem as much as a market-data problem.

More instruments → more updates.

More updates → more data to distribute, receive, and reconstruct.

And when updates are delayed, dropped, or arrive with variable timing, the resulting view of the book can differ from the underlying state.

So the interesting part of this launch isn't a promise about trading performance.

It's the infrastructure being built around the market.

A specialised data layer is emerging around an active onchain venue, with DoubleZero combining multicast, dedicated fiber, machine-readable feeds, and granular order-book data into Edge.

In simple terms:

Hyperliquid generates the market activity.

Edge is focused on how that activity gets delivered to systems that need to observe and reconstruct it.

That makes this a useful example of network infrastructure becoming part of the onchain market-data stack.

And importantly, the current announcement has a defined scope: native Hyperliquid perpetual markets and trade[XYZ] HIP-3 markets, across Market by Order and Top of Book feeds.

It should not be read as support for every future HIP-3 market or every Hyperliquid data product.

No token-price, trading-result, or profitability claims are needed to understand the significance of the infrastructure itself.

Source: DoubleZero announcement, 24 September 2026.

text:
$EQIX $DLR KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM THE ANTHROPIC–AKAMAI DEAL: EQUINIX AND DIGITAL REALTY

The deal is positive for both Equinix (EQIX: US) and Digital Realty (DLR: US), but the implications differ. Equinix receives the stronger incremental validation of its core investment thesis: substantial AI infrastructure demand can extend beyond large GPU campuses into CPU-based computing and interconnected deployment environments. Digital Realty receives another positive signal for large-scale capacity absorption, with potentially substantial direct leasing opportunities if Akamai concentrates the infrastructure in major campuses. The crucial distinction is that stronger strategic validation for Equinix does not establish that Equinix will capture more revenue than Digital Realty. Akamai’s announcement does not identify either company as a supplier, specify deployment locations, or disclose required megawatts. GlobeNewswire

The most important feature is the nature of the compute being purchased. Bloomberg describes the $11.6 billion, 7-year contract as access to CPUs supporting Anthropic’s AI services, expanding an earlier $1.8 billion agreement. This is evidence of substantial demand for infrastructure surrounding AI models—not evidence that large-model training or inference is broadly migrating from accelerators onto ordinary CPUs. Bloomberg Law

EQUINIX: A MORE DIRECT AI OPPORTUNITY FOR THE CORE COLOCATION BUSINESS

The strongest positive read-through for Equinix is that AI can generate meaningful demand for the types of computing environments supported by its existing colocation business, rather than requiring all incremental investment to flow into purpose-built GPU facilities.

Agentic applications combine model inference with code execution, tool calls, retrieval, memory management, and other processing. Research characterizing these applications finds materially different resource requirements from conventional model-serving workloads, including CPU execution and persistent memory requirements. The Anthropic contract provides a commercial signal consistent with that broader infrastructure requirement, although its detailed workload mix has not been disclosed. arXiv

The property-level implication is potentially attractive. Where a CPU deployment fits an existing facility’s electrical, cooling, networking, and floor-loading specifications, additional occupancy can be captured without the same retrofit requirements as an exceptionally dense accelerator deployment. Filling suitable, already-built capacity can produce better incremental returns than developing an entirely new facility.

That benefit is conditional, however. CPU-based does not automatically mean low-density, air-cooled, or compatible with every legacy data center. A large memory-intensive CPU installation can still require significant power and cooling. The favorable inference is that the range of potentially usable facilities may be broader—not that all older capacity suddenly becomes AI-ready.

Equinix’s September announcement of Inference Exchange with NVIDIA and Together AI also demonstrates that the company is already positioning around distributed AI infrastructure, with availability expected in Q1 2027. The Akamai deal reinforces the broader rationale for that strategy; it is not a customer award for that particular Equinix offering. Equinix, Inc.

Assessment: Meaningful positive strategic read-through for Equinix. Direct earnings magnitude remains unquantified until actual capacity commitments are identified.

EQUINIX: POTENTIAL INTERCONNECTION UPSIDE, BUT NOT A LINEAR CLAIM ON AI TRAFFIC

The next important implication is architectural. When model execution, CPU workers, data stores, cloud services, and enterprise applications reside across different environments, connectivity becomes part of the production system rather than merely a connection to the public internet.

Akamai’s own architectural discussion separates centralized heavy computation, regional inference, and CPU-based execution of tools and orchestration. That is the provider’s preferred architecture, not a disclosed map of Anthropic’s deployment. Nevertheless, it describes a plausible demand channel for Equinix: connecting multiple infrastructure environments efficiently and reliably. Akamai

Equinix can potentially monetize that through additional physical cross-connects, virtual connections, higher-capacity ports, and managed connectivity services. Its September Fabric One announcement explicitly targets connectivity across distributed environments, with AWS and Google Cloud participating in the initial integration work. A customer using several compute providers creates more potential connection points than a workload entirely contained within a single provider’s internal network. Equinix, Inc.

The limiting factor is monetization. More agent calls or more data traffic do not automatically create proportionate interconnection revenue. A few large connections may carry substantial additional traffic before another paid service or capacity tier is required. Likewise, a large CPU cluster connected to a nearby model-serving cluster could be economically important without producing thousands of new cross-connects.

There is a documented historical Akamai–Equinix relationship: a 2020 joint discussion described Akamai security scrubbing centers hosted on Platform Equinix and connected through its exchange fabric. That establishes commercial familiarity and an existing infrastructure relationship, but it does not establish that Anthropic’s new CPU capacity will be hosted there. Equinix Blog

Assessment: Positive, potentially high-quality incremental revenue for Equinix where connectivity is sold alongside capacity. More uncertain in magnitude than the general CPU-demand signal.

DIGITAL REALTY: POTENTIALLY LARGER DIRECT CAPACITY WINS IF DEPLOYMENTS ARE CONCENTRATED

Digital Realty’s clearest opportunity is the physical capacity required to support large-scale CPU deployment. Its offering spans enterprise colocation, dedicated suites, powered buildings, and build-to-suit facilities. That breadth gives it a plausible role whether Akamai purchases smaller blocks of capacity or establishes larger dedicated deployments. Digital Realty Trust

The most important analytical caution is that “distributed infrastructure” does not necessarily mean numerous small edge facilities. A service can be geographically distributed across a limited number of large regional campuses. CPU capacity can also be concentrated near model-serving infrastructure, important data stores, or major cloud regions rather than near individual end users.

Under that configuration, Digital Realty could capture more direct rental dollars than Equinix even though the announcement provides a sharper narrative benefit to Equinix. The relevant variables are the size of each deployment, required delivery date, available power, network adjacency, and price—not whether the hardware contains CPUs rather than GPUs.

The potential financial transmission is straightforward: additional leased capacity increases occupancy or supports preleasing of development projects; contracted capacity reduces the risk of building without a tenant; and successful delivery eventually generates rental income and operating cash flow. The attractive outcome is not simply more construction. It is additional leasing at returns that adequately compensate for development spending and financing costs.

Digital Realty also should not be treated as exclusively a large-campus business. ServiceFabric connects workloads with clouds, model providers, networks, and other locations. The interconnection thesis therefore benefits both companies, even though it is more central to the conventional Equinix investment framework. Digital Realty

Assessment: Positive fundamental demand read-through for Digital Realty, with potentially substantial individual lease awards. No disclosed evidence currently establishes the size of its participation.

BOTH COMPANIES: AKAMAI IS A POTENTIAL CUSTOMER CHANNEL, NOT NECESSARILY A COMPETITIVE THREAT

The transaction illustrates why a cloud provider winning business need not be negative for data-center landlords. Akamai supplies compute services, software, and operations. Equinix and Digital Realty can supply the underlying facilities, power infrastructure, and connectivity. These activities occupy different portions of the infrastructure stack.

Equinix’s announced Inference Exchange explicitly illustrates this division of responsibilities: Equinix provides the infrastructure foundation, while a separate provider operates the AI platform above it. Digital Realty similarly markets facilities and interconnection to both enterprises and service providers. The read-through is that growth in alternative cloud providers can expand the potential tenant base rather than bypass it. Equinix, Inc.

There are 2 distinct scenarios. If Akamai leases incremental space and power to satisfy Anthropic, the landlord benefits directly. If Akamai places the workload inside capacity it already pays for, the immediate economic benefit accrues primarily to Akamai through improved utilization; the landlord may receive little additional revenue until Akamai expands.

Consequently, the useful signal is not simply that Anthropic selected a provider outside the largest public clouds. It is whether that provider’s expansion requires new third-party facility commitments.

For both landlords, this also reinforces the value of remaining neutral across compute architectures and service providers. A landlord can potentially earn rent regardless of which model, processor architecture, or cloud operator wins, provided the winning workloads run within its facilities.

THE $11.6 BILLION HEADLINE CANNOT BE TRANSLATED DIRECTLY INTO LANDLORD REVENUE

Akamai estimates approximately $5.5 billion of capital expenditures associated with the base commitment, including an additional approximately $1.7 billion in 2026 to secure critical components such as memory. The transaction also allows a further $9 billion expansion, but that additional amount is not equivalent to the initial contractual commitment. GlobeNewswire

For Equinix and Digital Realty, 3 different economic measures must remain separate: Anthropic’s spending on cloud services, Akamai’s investment in compute infrastructure, and the landlord’s revenue from facilities and connectivity. Neither the cloud contract value nor Akamai’s capital budget is a data-center construction budget.

The appropriate earnings bridge starts with the incremental power capacity actually leased at each landlord, the rental or colocation rate, the commencement schedule, and any associated services. Operating costs, landlord-funded improvements, financing, and joint-venture ownership then determine the contribution to shareholders. Electricity reimbursements also should not be treated as equivalent to high-margin rental growth.

This distinction matters particularly when hardware is expensive. A large increase in memory or server spending can raise the contract’s dollar value without an equivalent increase in required facility capacity. Conversely, substantial deployment across many modestly sized locations can create valuable colocation and connectivity revenue without resembling a single enormous campus lease.

The strongest outcome would be incremental demand filling already-available, appropriately powered capacity. A less attractive outcome would require substantial speculative development or unusually expensive upgrades. The deal’s size alone does not establish which outcome either landlord will experience.

THE MAIN NEGATIVE READ-THROUGHS ARE CONCENTRATION, DOUBLE COUNTING, AND CONTRACT MISMATCH

The largest portfolio-level risk is confusing diversification of suppliers with diversification of underlying demand. Anthropic can purchase capacity through several infrastructure providers while remaining the ultimate economic driver behind all those deployments. A landlord may therefore appear diversified across named tenants while having greater indirect exposure to the same model developer or workload than tenant disclosures suggest.

That is a concentration issue, not evidence that the demand is artificial. It requires examining the legal tenant, guarantees, deposits, termination rights, and the tenant’s ability to support its lease obligations independently of a particular end customer.

The commercial terms also deserve attention. Akamai issued a warrant that can cover approximately 5% of its outstanding common shares on an as-converted basis, with vesting linked to the initial commitment and subsequent expansion. This demonstrates that the cloud contract includes an equity component; headline service revenue is not a complete measure of Akamai’s economic return. It does not imply that Equinix or Digital Realty must offer similar concessions, but it argues against assuming every large AI contract has equally attractive underlying economics. CNA

There is also a potential maturity mismatch. A 7-year compute arrangement does not automatically provide a landlord with a matching 7-year, fully protected rental stream. That depends on the separate facility contract. For new construction, the important question is whether the lease, customer credit, and residual value of the facility justify the investment—not simply whether the end customer has announced a long-duration purchase.

Finally, some demand could represent relocation from another provider rather than wholly incremental industry capacity. The transaction is clearly positive evidence of Anthropic’s willingness to commit to infrastructure, but it should not be counted as entirely additive to every existing cloud and data-center forecast.

NEAR-TERM STOCK IMPLICATIONS VERSUS LONGER-TERM EARNINGS

Near-term, the announcement is more useful as a demand and architecture catalyst than as a basis for immediate earnings revisions. Reported comments from Akamai’s CEO indicate an expected service start in H2 2027, approximately $150 million–$300 million of Anthropic revenue in 2027, and an annual run rate of approximately $1.7 billion by 2028. Facility commitments and development spending can precede that service revenue, but the landlord-specific timing remains undisclosed. TNW

For Equinix, this is reinforcement of an already improving operating narrative rather than the first evidence of AI-related opportunity. Its Q2 release reported $424 million of annualized gross bookings, 23% growth in gross bookings, and a record 9,700 net interconnection additions. It also raised its 2027–2029 outlook to 10%–13% annual revenue growth and 9%–12% annual AFFO-per-share growth. The incremental investment question is whether this broader CPU opportunity produces upside to those expectations—not simply whether it supports them. Equinix, Inc.

For Digital Realty, the most consequential confirmation would be new leasing and commencement disclosures showing that alternative-cloud CPU deployments are translating into capacity absorption. For both companies, signed contracts, delivery schedules, incremental landlord capital requirements, and ownership-adjusted cash flow are more informative than another general statement that AI demand remains strong.

INVESTMENT CONCLUSION

Equinix has the stronger incremental strategic read-through: the deal supports the proposition that meaningful AI value can accrue to interconnected colocation infrastructure, not only to enormous accelerator campuses. Its potential upside comes from a combination of capacity utilization and connectivity.

Digital Realty has a clear positive fundamental read-through and could ultimately capture the larger direct rental opportunity if deployment is concentrated in large facilities. CPU-based infrastructure is fully compatible with a large-campus leasing model; distributed computing and hyperscale facilities are not mutually exclusive.

The appropriate conclusion is positive for both, with greater thematic significance for Equinix and potentially greater large-block leasing sensitivity for Digital Realty. The announcement alone does not establish a relative earnings winner or justify a specific FFO/AFFO increase. The decisive evidence will be where Akamai places the equipment, how much incremental capacity it contracts, and the returns earned by the landlord supplying it.

text:
$AKAM Akamai and Anthropic: A Strategic Shift to AI Computing Infrastructure. Investment Thesis. New: 9/24/26.

Akamai's Anthropic agreement is the most consequential strategic decision in the company's history — not because of its scale alone, but because of what it signals about the strategic direction management is choosing. Committing $5.5 billion in capital investment to build general-purpose computing infrastructure for a single AI customer transforms Akamai from a mature, cash-generative CDN and security business into a capital-intensive infrastructure provider with a concentrated customer dependency. That transformation may ultimately create more value than the legacy model, but it requires underwriting a fundamentally different risk profile than Akamai investors have historically owned.

The legacy business — content delivery and security — is a genuinely cash-generative franchise with defensible market positions and predictable revenue characteristics. The free cash flow that business has produced is the financial foundation being redirected toward the Anthropic infrastructure buildout, and the near-term cash flow compression that $5.5 billion in capital investment creates is real and substantial. The period between capital deployment and revenue commencement in late 2027 is the financial gap that incremental financing needs to bridge — and the ability to secure that financing on terms that don't excessively dilute existing shareholders or encumber the balance sheet is the near-term execution requirement that sits before the operational questions.

The shareholder warrant linking equity value to the partnership's success is the governance mechanism that aligns Anthropic's incentives with Akamai's long-term performance — but it also introduces an equity overhang whose dilutive impact depends on the stock price trajectory during the warrant exercise window. Warrant structures of this kind are standard in large commercial partnerships, but their effect on per-share value needs to be modeled explicitly rather than treated as a neutral feature of the deal structure.

Customer concentration is the structural risk that the contract scale creates almost by definition. An $11.6 billion agreement with a single counterparty means that Akamai's infrastructure business is essentially a bilateral relationship for the foreseeable future — the revenue visibility is exceptional, but the dependence on Anthropic's operational success, financial health, and strategic continuity is total. Anthropic's own trajectory — its competitive position in AI model development, its revenue growth, and its capital structure — becomes a direct input into Akamai's infrastructure business performance in ways that external monitoring rather than internal execution determines.

The operational execution requirements are substantial on their own merits. Building and operating general-purpose computing infrastructure at the scale the agreement requires is a different capability than CDN node deployment and security software delivery. The engineering, procurement, and operations talent required to execute a $5.5 billion infrastructure buildout on a compressed timeline while simultaneously managing the legacy business is an organizational stretch that needs to be resourced explicitly rather than assumed to be addressable with the existing team.

The long-term value creation thesis depends on the Anthropic relationship producing the revenue and margin profile that justifies both the capital investment and the strategic redirection — and on that relationship serving as a proof of concept that attracts additional AI infrastructure customers rather than remaining a single concentrated dependency. Whether the first enables the second is the strategic question that determines whether this is a transformative platform pivot or a very large bilateral contract.

Her message contained one sentence:

Please do not contact working crew during flight unless it concerns passenger safety.

I read it three times.

Maya saw my face.

“She texted you?”

“Daniel.”

I locked the phone.

Maya reached for her bag.

“What are you doing?”

“Moving seats.”

“You can’t.”

“I absolutely can.”

She pressed the call button.

My stomach dropped.

Sarah appeared less than thirty seconds later.

“Yes, ma’am?”

Maya looked directly at her.

“Is there another open seat?”

Sarah’s expression did not change.

“I can check.”

“I’d prefer not to sit here.”

There was a pause.

Short.

Professional.

Loaded.

“Of course,” Sarah said. “Let me see what’s available.”

I wanted to disappear.

The man in 2C looked down at his coffee with the unnatural concentration of someone desperate not to be involved. The woman across the aisle pretended to read but had not turned a page in ten minutes.

Sarah returned.

“There’s an open aisle seat in row seven. Still in the premium cabin. I can help move your bag.”

Maya stood immediately.

“Maya,” I whispered.

She looked down at me.

“Don’t.”

That one word had more dignity than any explanation I could have offered.

Sarah helped her retrieve her bag from the overhead bin. Their hands briefly touched when Sarah handed over the coat Maya had refused earlier. Neither woman flinched. I watched them walk away together, my wife and my mistress, and realized I had made enemies of two women who should never have been placed in competition.

A few minutes later, Sarah returned to the front cabin.

She leaned slightly toward me, still smiling in that professional way.

“Mr. Mercer, please keep your seat belt fastened while seated.”

My belt was already fastened.

She knew that.

The sentence was not about safety.

It was about control.

For the first time in our marriage, Sarah had all of it.

The next two hours were slow punishment.

Not loud.

Not cruel.

Worse.

Civil.

Sarah served meals. She checked on passengers. She helped a child with headphones. She laughed politely at an elderly man’s joke. She gave Maya the same level of service she gave everyone else no less, no more.

That was what made me sick.

She refused to make herself small, hysterical, or unprofessional to match the size of my betrayal.

I tried to rehearse what I would say when we landed.

I was going to explain that things had been bad between us.

That I felt lonely.

That Maya made me feel alive.

That I never meant for Sarah to find out like this.

Every version sounded cowardly even in my own head.

Because the truth was not that I had fallen helplessly into an affair.

I had scheduled it.

Budgeted it.

Lied around it.

Charged meals to business accounts.

Used Sarah’s layovers as opportunities.

Used her trust as infrastructure.

At some point over Kansas, Kelly the other flight attendant leaned toward Sarah in the galley. They whispered. Kelly looked briefly at me, then away. I wondered how much she knew. Flight crews talk. They are trained observers. Sarah could probably have told her everything without raising her voice.

Then Maya came back.

Not to sit.

To stand in the aisle beside my seat.

Her face was pale but composed.

“We need to talk.”

“Not here.”

Her mouth tightened.

“Of course.”

I glanced toward the galley.

Sarah was watching.

Maya followed my gaze and laughed once.

“You are still more worried about being seen than what you did.”….
